title: Writing with precision
goals: Nominalise and condense information with the correct preposition (an increase in, demand for).
Grade the strength of your claims with advanced hedging, without stacking hedges.
Achieve cohesion through reference, connectors and information focus.
Summarise and synthesise several sources by reconstructing their arguments.
Use C2 academic vocabulary accurately (substantiate, discrepancy, ubiquitous).

learn.title: Nominalisation: density and academic objectivity
learn.html:
Nominalisation consists of turning a verb, an adjective or even a whole clause into a noun. In academic prose it performs three functions: it condenses information (an entire clause fits into a noun phrase), it depersonalises the statement (the focus shifts from people to processes) and it allows what has already been said to become the starting point of the next sentence (This decline…).

Verbal version (conversational)Nominalised version (academic)
Prices rose sharply, so people spent less.The sharp rise in prices led to a reduction in consumer spending.
Because the committee failed to act, the crisis worsened.The committee's failure to act exacerbated the crisis.
Researchers analyzed the data carefully.A careful analysis of the data was undertaken.
Teachers are reluctant to change.Teachers' reluctance to change is well documented.

Prepositions that accompany the noun (inherited from the verb or adjective, but not always the same as in Spanish): an increase/decrease/rise/fall in unemployment (what changes), but an increase of 3% (by how much); demand for, a lack of, emphasis on, an approach to, reliance on, a shift towards, a discrepancy between.

"Light" verbs that connect noun phrases: lead to, result in, give rise to, account for, contribute to, stem from, be attributable to. Use them instead of because / so to chain causes and effects.

Caution: overusing nominalisation produces heavy prose (the carrying out of the implementation of the evaluation). Keep the agent visible when it matters who did what.

watch.wrong: The analyze of the data took six months.
watch.right: The analysis of the data took six months.
watch.why: Analyze is the verb; the noun is analysis. A frequent error when building noun phrases from the base verb.

watch.wrong: There was an increase of unemployment.
watch.right: There was an increase in unemployment.
watch.why: Increase in + what changes; increase of only introduces the quantity (an increase of 3%).

watch.wrong: The importance of to reduce emissions is clear.
watch.right: The importance of reducing emissions is clear.
watch.why: After a preposition comes a gerund or a noun, never an infinitive with "to".
After a possessive a noun is needed (decision), not the verb.

learn.title: Advanced hedging
learn.html:
Hedging is the set of resources by which an author grades their commitment to what they assert. It is not weakness: in academic writing it is epistemic precision. Asserting more than the data allow is a methodological error; asserting less is simply prudence.

ResourceExamples
Modal verbsmay, might, could, would, should: This may reflect a broader trend.
Lexical verbs of cautionseem, appear, tend, suggest, indicate, imply: The data suggest that…
Adverbs of degree/probabilityarguably, presumably, conceivably, largely, somewhat, broadly
Approximatorsroughly, in the region of, to some extent, in the main, a proportion of
Impersonal structuresIt would appear that…; There is some evidence to suggest that…; It is conceivable that…

Patterns: seem/appear + to + infinitive (The results seem to be reliable), with a perfect infinitive for the past (seems to have declined); It seems/appears that + clause; tend to + infinitive; a tendency for + subject + to + infinitive.

Two calibration principles. (1) Choose reporting verbs that match the strength of the evidence: suggest < indicate < demonstrate < prove (the last is almost avoided outside mathematics). (2) Do not stack hedges: It may possibly perhaps suggest… sounds clumsy; one is enough, or two of different types (It may, to some extent, reflect…).

watch.wrong: The results seem that they are reliable.
watch.right: The results seem to be reliable. / It seems that the results are reliable.
watch.why: Seem is built with to + infinitive, with an adjective, or with "it seems that"; not with "that" + its own subject.

watch.wrong: This might possibly perhaps indicate a trend.
watch.why: Piling up hedges is redundant and reduces credibility; one is enough.

watch.wrong: The data prove that the drug is effective.
watch.right: The data suggest that the drug is effective.
watch.why: Prove expresses absolute certainty; in empirical science suggest or indicate is preferred.

watch.wrong: There is a tendency of students to procrastinate.
watch.right: There is a tendency for students to procrastinate.
watch.why: With its own subject the structure is a tendency for + subject + to; a tendency of does not fit.

learn.title: Cohesion: reference, linking and information focus
learn.html:
A cohesive academic text guides the reader through two principles: known information first, new information at the end (end-focus), and an explicit system of reference and connectors.

FunctionResources
Summarising the previous point with a nounThis trend / this shift / this discrepancy / such a view / these findings (demonstrative + noun that labels what was said; avoid bare this when it could refer to several things)
Picking up two elementsthe former / the latter (only when there are exactly two), respectively
Cause/justificationgiven that, in view of, owing to the fact that, inasmuch as
Contrast/concessionwhereas, while, albeit, notwithstanding, even so, that said
Chained consequence…, thereby + -ing; …, whereby + clause; hence, thus, consequently
Delimiting scopeinsofar as, to the extent that, in so far as the data allow

Clause reduction: as mentioned above, as shown in Table 2 (not as it was mentioned). Despite / in spite of + noun or gerund, with no of after despite. Due to the fact requires that.

watch.wrong: Despite of the delays, the project was completed.
watch.right: Despite the delays, the project was completed. / In spite of the delays, …

watch.wrong: Due to the fact the sample was small, the results are tentative.
watch.right: Due to the fact that the sample was small, the results are tentative.
watch.why: The phrase is due to the fact that; better still, simplify with because or given that.

watch.wrong: As it was mentioned above, costs have risen.
watch.right: As mentioned above, costs have risen.
watch.why: In academic English the clause is reduced: as mentioned / as noted / as discussed above.

watch.wrong: Of the three proposals, the former is the cheapest.
watch.right: Of the three proposals, the first is the cheapest.
watch.why: The former / the latter only work with two elements; with three or more use first, second, third.

learn.title: Summarising and synthesising several sources
learn.html:
Summarising at a mastery level is not shortening a text: it is reconstructing its argument (claim → evidence → implication) in your own words and, when synthesising several sources, putting them in conversation rather than summarising them one after another.

Stance of the cited authorVerbs
Neutralstate, report, note, observe, describe, outline
Firmargue, assert, maintain, contend, insist, hold that
Cautioussuggest, propose, speculate, hypothesize, tentatively conclude
Writer's distanceclaim, purport, allege (the writer doubts the assertion)
Established factdemonstrate, establish, reveal, show

Synthesis structures: While Reyes (2021) contends that…, Lund (2022) found no such effect; Both studies concur that…, but diverge on…; By contrast, …; Taken together, these studies suggest…; Collectively, the literature points to…. To open a summary: The article sets out to examine…; The central argument is that…. Reporting verbs go in the simple present (Smith argues) or the present perfect when current relevance matters.

Your own stance: In my view / In my opinion (never according to me); According to X is reserved for other people's sources. Avoid literal copying: change the syntactic structure, not just the synonyms.

watch.wrong: According to me, the policy has failed.
watch.right: In my view, the policy has failed.
watch.why: According to attributes a view to another source; for your own stance: in my view / in my opinion.

watch.wrong: Both authors agree in that funding is inadequate.
watch.right: Both authors agree that funding is inadequate.
watch.why: Agree that + clause; "in that" is not used as the Spanish "en que" would be.

watch.wrong: The report emphasizes on the need for transparency.
watch.right: The report emphasizes the need for transparency.
watch.why: Emphasize / stress / underline are transitive; emphasis on does take "on" (noun).

watch.wrong: The author demonstrates that maybe the effect exists.
watch.right: The author suggests that the effect may exist.
watch.why: Demonstrate is factive (it presents something as proven); with an uncertain conclusion use suggest.

learn.title: Signposting and synthesis language
learn.html:
Opening and delimiting: This paper sets out to… / The central argument is that… / The scope of this study is limited to…

Qualifying a finding: The findings are broadly consistent with… / To some extent, … / This is not to say that… / It would be premature to conclude that…

Acknowledging limits: One important caveat is… / These results should be interpreted with caution, given that… / A limitation of this approach is…

Putting sources in dialogue: While X contends…, Y maintains… / Both accounts concur that…, yet they diverge on… / Taken together, these studies suggest…

Distinguishing and relating: draw a distinction between… / shed light on… / lend support to… / give rise to… / take into account… / bear out the claim that…

Concluding with restraint: In the light of the above, … / On balance, … / Further research would be needed to establish whether…

practice.title: Nominalisation
practice.instructions: Complete, choose or correct to achieve a dense and correct academic style.

items.prompt: Prices rose sharply, which led to a reduction in spending. = The sharp ___ in prices led to a reduction in spending.
answers: rise
increase
items.explain: Verb rose → noun rise / increase, followed by "in prices".

items.prompt: Because the committee failed to act, the crisis worsened. = The committee's ___ to act worsened the crisis.
items.explain: After a possessive a noun is needed: failure.

items.prompt: The researchers analyzed the samples carefully. = A careful ___ of the samples was carried out.
answers: analysis
items.explain: The noun from analyze is analysis (plural analyses).

items.prompt: There has been a significant increase of unemployment among graduates.
answers: There has been a significant increase in unemployment among graduates.
items.explain: Increase in + what changes; "of" only introduces the quantity.

items.prompt: There is growing demand ___ affordable housing.
items.explain: Demand for: the noun keeps the preposition "for".

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: The expansion of the network led to improved access.
items.explain: Subject noun phrase (expansion of the network) + light verb "led to" + noun phrase.

items.prompt: Teachers are reluctant to change. = Teachers' ___ to change is well documented.
answers: reluctance
items.explain: Adjective reluctant → noun reluctance.

items.prompt: Which version is most typical of nominalised academic style?
options: Because people spent less, firms sold fewer goods.
The reduction in consumer spending resulted in lower sales.
People spent less so firms sold less.
items.explain: Nominalisation condenses clauses into noun phrases linked by a light verb (resulted in).

practice.title: Advanced hedging
practice.instructions: Choose or complete to calibrate the strength of the claim.

items.prompt: The findings ___ that sleep affects memory, though more research is needed.
items.explain: With evidence that is still provisional, use "suggest"; "prove" would be too absolute.

items.prompt: It would ___ that the early estimates were too optimistic.
answers: appear
seem
items.explain: "It would appear/seem that…": an impersonal structure of caution.

items.prompt: The results seem that they are reliable.
answers: The results seem to be reliable.
It seems that the results are reliable.
The results seem reliable.
items.explain: Seem + to + infinitive, + adjective, or "it seems that" + clause.

items.prompt: Social media ___ anxiety in some adolescents.
items.explain: "May contribute to" softens the causality and limits the scope (some adolescents).

items.prompt: There is a tendency ___ students to underestimate the time a task requires.
answers: for
items.explain: A tendency for + subject + to + infinitive.

items.prompt: This might possibly perhaps indicate a wider problem.
answers: This might indicate a wider problem.
This may indicate a wider problem.
This could indicate a wider problem.
Perhaps this indicates a wider problem.
This possibly indicates a wider problem.
items.explain: A single hedge is enough; stacking them sounds clumsy.

items.prompt: The new policy has ___ reduced waiting times, although the data are incomplete.
items.explain: "Arguably" marks a defensible but not indisputable claim; the other two express certainty.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: To a large extent, the results support the hypothesis.
items.explain: "To a large extent" works as an approximator at the start of the sentence.

practice.title: Cohesion and connectors
practice.instructions: Choose, complete or correct to achieve academic cohesion.

items.prompt: Two options were considered: remote work and a four-day week. Of the two, the ___ proved cheaper.
items.explain: "The latter" picks up the second of two elements (a four-day week).

items.prompt: ___ that the sample was small, the conclusions should be treated with caution.
answers: given
considering
seeing
items.explain: Given that + clause introduces the justification.

items.prompt: Due to the fact the sample was small, the results are tentative.
answers: Due to the fact that the sample was small, the results are tentative.
Owing to the fact that the sample was small, the results are tentative.
Because the sample was small, the results are tentative.
Given that the sample was small, the results are tentative.
items.explain: "Due to the fact" requires "that"; or simplify with "because" / "given that".

items.prompt: The government cut subsidies, ___ widening the gap between rural and urban incomes.
items.explain: "Thereby" + -ing expresses a result derived from the previous action.

items.prompt: The first and second studies involved 40 and 400 participants, ___.
answers: respectively
items.explain: "Respectively" links the elements in the same order.

items.prompt: Despite of the delays, the project was completed on schedule.
answers: Despite the delays, the project was completed on schedule.
In spite of the delays, the project was completed on schedule.
items.explain: "Despite" takes no "of"; "in spite of" does.

items.prompt: Profits fell by 20% last year. ___ decline prompted a full review.
items.explain: Demonstrative + noun that labels what was said (this decline).

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: Insofar as the data allow, the trend appears stable.
items.explain: "Insofar as" delimits the scope of the claim.

practice.title: Summarising and synthesising
practice.instructions: Choose or correct to report sources accurately.

items.prompt: According to Reyes (2021), remote work boosts productivity. ___, Lund (2022) found no such effect.
items.explain: "By contrast" marks a contrast between two sources.

items.prompt: According to me, the policy has failed.
answers: In my view, the policy has failed.
In my opinion, the policy has failed.
items.explain: Your own stance: "in my view" / "in my opinion".

items.prompt: Both authors agree in that funding is inadequate.
answers: Both authors agree that funding is inadequate.
Both authors concur that funding is inadequate.
items.explain: "Agree that" + clause.

items.prompt: The company ___ that its product is harmless, but independent tests disagree.
items.explain: "Claim" distances the writer from the assertion; "demonstrate" and "establish" present it as true.

items.prompt: While Park argues that wages are the main factor, Okoye ___ that housing costs matter more.
items.explain: "Maintains": a firm stance verb, suitable for contrasting authors.

items.prompt: The report emphasizes on the need for transparency.
answers: The report emphasizes the need for transparency.
The report stresses the need for transparency.
The report underlines the need for transparency.
The report highlights the need for transparency.
items.explain: "Emphasize" is transitive: no "on".

items.prompt: Which is the best opening for an academic summary?
options: The article sets out to examine why…
I want to tell you what the article says about…
In the article there is a topic that…
items.explain: "The article sets out to…" is the standard opening format for a summary.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: Taken together, these studies suggest a modest effect.
items.explain: "Taken together" synthesises several sources; "suggest" moderates the conclusion.

practice.title: Academic verbs
practice.instructions: Choose, complete or correct with the precise verb.

items.prompt: The leaked emails ___ the minister's account, since they contradict it.
items.explain: Undermine = to weaken; "corroborate" would confirm her account.

items.prompt: Independent witnesses ___ her version of events, confirming every detail. (corroborate)
answers: corroborated
items.explain: Corroborate = to confirm with another source (past).

items.prompt: The author ___ to earlier work without naming it.
items.explain: Allude to = to refer indirectly.

items.prompt: Rising rents have ___ the housing shortage. (exacerbate)
answers: exacerbated
items.explain: Exacerbate = to worsen (present perfect).

items.prompt: The commission will ascertain to the cause of the fire.
answers: The commission will ascertain the cause of the fire.
items.explain: Ascertain is transitive: no "to".

items.prompt: The term 'sustainability' ___ economic, social and environmental concerns.
items.explain: Encompass = to include, to cover.

items.prompt: Strict regulations ___ small firms from entering the market.
answers: preclude
prevent
bar
deter
items.explain: Preclude somebody from -ing: to prevent someone from doing something.

items.prompt: Critics accuse the company of trying to ___ safety rules.
items.explain: Circumvent = to get around a rule without openly breaking it.

items.prompt: There is a marked ___ between the official figures and those collected by the NGO.
items.explain: Discrepancy between X and Y = a gap between the two.

items.prompt: Smartphones are now ___: you will find them in almost every pocket in the world.
answers: ubiquitous
pervasive
items.explain: Ubiquitous = present everywhere.

items.prompt: The link between the two events is ___, so we should not rely on it.
items.explain: Tenuous = weak, flimsy.

items.prompt: The proliferation of fake accounts have made fact-checking essential.
answers: The proliferation of fake accounts has made fact-checking essential.
items.explain: The subject's head noun is "proliferation" (singular): has made.

items.prompt: The scandal gave fresh ___ to calls for reform.
answers: impetus
items.explain: Give impetus to = to give momentum to.

items.prompt: A quiet environment is ___ to concentration.
items.explain: Conducive to = favourable to.

items.prompt: The ___ behind the reform was to reduce costs.
items.explain: Rationale = the reason behind something, the justification.

items.prompt: There is one important ___ to these findings: the sample was drawn from a single city.
answers: caveat
items.explain: Caveat = a qualification or warning.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: The decision to withdraw was taken without consultation.
items.explain: Noun phrase subject + passive.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: It would appear that the figures were overstated.
items.explain: Impersonal hedging structure.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: There is some evidence to suggest that sleep aids memory.
items.explain: "There is some evidence to suggest that…" softens the claim.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: The former argues for reform, whereas the latter favours stability.
items.explain: "The former / the latter" with two elements; "whereas" contrasts.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: Given the scale of the problem, no single solution is sufficient.
items.explain: "Given" + noun phrase introduces the justification.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: A rise in interest rates may well curb inflation.
items.explain: "May well" = it is very possible that.

write.prompt: Write a short academic essay (300 to 400 words) that answers this question: "To what extent does remote work improve productivity?" Present a nuanced thesis, two arguments supported by hypothetical evidence (cite invented sources such as Reyes (2021)) and one caveat. Use nominalisation, hedging and cohesive connectors. Opening example: The question of whether remote work enhances productivity admits of no simple answer…
targets: nominalization (the rise in…, the failure to…)
hedging (suggest, may, to some extent, arguably)
cohesion (this + noun, the former/the latter, whereas, thereby + -ing)
checklist: Between 300 and 400 words
A clear, nuanced thesis in the introduction
At least 5 well-formed nominalisations with their preposition (increase in, demand for…)
At least 4 different hedging resources, without stacking them
At least 3 varied cohesive connectors and 1 "this + noun"
Reporting verbs matched to the strength of the evidence
3 or more words from the unit's academic list
A final paragraph with limits and lines of future research
write.model:
The question of whether remote work enhances productivity admits of no simple answer. The evidence suggests that the effect is positive for some tasks and some workers, yet the extent of the improvement depends on how productivity is defined and measured. This essay argues that remote work may raise individual output to some extent, but that its benefits are arguably offset where collaboration is central.

The first argument concerns focus. Reyes (2021), in a study of 800 software developers, found that the reduction in interruptions at home was associated with a rise in completed tasks of roughly twelve per cent. The absence of a daily commute, which the author estimates at ninety minutes, appears to contribute further to this increase in available working time. Whereas the productivity gain is substantial, it rests on self-reported hours, which are notoriously imprecise.

The second argument relates to motivation and autonomy. Okafor and Lind (2022) contend that greater control over one's schedule heightens engagement, thereby reducing turnover and the costs it entails. The former effect is plausible; the latter is better documented, as the decline in resignations among remote staff has been replicated across several firms. This pattern could indicate that retention, rather than raw output, is the principal gain.

A significant caveat must nevertheless be recognised. The same literature points to a discrepancy between routine and creative work: Tanaka (2020) reports that the failure to exchange ideas informally impairs innovation in teams that never meet. This suggests that the benefits of remote work may be unevenly distributed, and that a firm which treats productivity as a single quantity risks mistaking efficiency for effectiveness.

In conclusion, the balance of evidence indicates that remote work probably improves productivity under certain conditions, but it cannot yet substantiate a general claim. The samples in most studies are drawn from technology firms, which limits generalisability, and few examine long-term effects. Future research should therefore compare sectors, follow workers over several years, and distinguish between output and quality, so that the conclusions drawn can be more securely grounded.

write.prompt: Synthesise three sources in a text of 300 to 400 words. Source A (Moreno, 2020): a survey of 2,000 students concludes that sleeping fewer than six hours reduces exam performance. Source B (Chen and Ibarra, 2022): an experiment with 120 participants found a small effect, and only on memory tasks. Source C (Hartley, 2023): a review of 40 studies maintains that the effect exists, but that it depends on age and on how performance is measured. Do not summarise one source after another: put them in dialogue, point out where they agree and diverge, and close with a measured conclusion.
targets: synthesis of sources (while…, both concur that…, by contrast)
checklist: Between 300 and 400 words
The three sources are integrated, not presented in separate blocks
At least one contrast (while / whereas / by contrast) and one point of agreement (both concur that)
Varied reporting verbs matched to the strength of the evidence
"Taken together" / "collectively" in the conclusion
Hedging in the conclusion (suggest, may, to some extent)
A caveat about sample size or method
Your own stance with "In my view", not "According to me"
write.model:
The relationship between sleep and academic performance is often assumed to be straightforward, yet the three studies considered here, taken together, tell a more qualified story.

All three sources concur that short sleep is associated with some decline in performance, but they diverge sharply over its size and scope. Moreno (2020), surveying 2,000 students, concludes that sleeping fewer than six hours reduces exam results; by contrast, Chen and Ibarra (2022), whose experiment involved only 120 participants, found a small effect, and one confined to memory tasks. The discrepancy is instructive. A large survey can detect broad patterns, whereas a controlled experiment can isolate causes, and it may be that each is capturing a different part of the same phenomenon. Moreover, a survey can show an association but not a cause: students who sleep little may also be busier or more stressed, so poor results are not necessarily the product of lack of sleep.

Hartley (2023) goes some way towards reconciling the two. Reviewing forty studies, she maintains that the effect is real but conditional, depending on the age of the participants and on how performance is measured. This would explain why Chen and Ibarra, who tested a narrow task, observed a modest result, while Moreno, who looked at overall exam marks, observed a larger one. Hartley's review is, however, only as strong as the studies it includes, and it does not settle whether the variation lies in the effect itself or in the research methods.

Two caveats deserve mention. First, the sample in Chen and Ibarra's experiment is small, so their results may not generalise. Second, self-reported sleep, which surveys of this kind commonly rely on, is notoriously unreliable.

Taken together, the sources suggest that insufficient sleep probably does impair performance to some extent, particularly in memory-dependent tasks, but that the magnitude is likely to vary with age and with the measure employed. In my view, the evidence justifies encouraging students to sleep adequately, yet it does not support the claim that sleep alone determines how well they do.

reading.title: The Replication Crisis: How Much Can We Trust a Single Study?
reading.intro: Read the article and answer the questions. Notice how the author grades each claim.
paragraphs: In 2015, a consortium of psychologists published the results of an unusual undertaking: they had attempted to reproduce one hundred experiments that had appeared in leading journals. Fewer than half of the replications yielded results that matched the originals. The announcement was widely interpreted as evidence of a crisis, yet the term obscures as much as it reveals. What the episode exposed was not so much widespread fraud as a set of habits, many of them well-intentioned, that make it easy for an unreliable finding to acquire the aura of established fact.

Consider the incentives. Academic careers are built on publications, and journals have historically favoured studies that report a statistically significant effect over those that find nothing. A researcher who runs an experiment and detects no difference between groups faces a discouraging prospect: the result is hard to publish and therefore, from a career perspective, almost worthless. The temptation, which few researchers would openly admit to, is to keep looking: to test an additional variable, to exclude a handful of 'anomalous' participants, or to adjust the analysis until a pattern emerges. Each choice can be defended individually; collectively, they inflate the likelihood of a false positive.

This practice, sometimes called p-hacking, is rarely deliberate in any crude sense. It tends to arise from the ordinary flexibility of data analysis, in which dozens of defensible decisions must be made before a single number is reported. The proliferation of such decisions, what one statistician has termed the 'garden of forking paths', means that two honest analysts can reach divergent conclusions from identical data. The discrepancy is not evidence of incompetence; it is an inherent feature of the process, and one that conventional peer review is poorly equipped to detect, since reviewers typically see only the finished analysis, not the paths that were abandoned.

Reform has nonetheless gained considerable momentum. A growing number of journals now offer 'registered reports', in which the methodology is reviewed and accepted before any data are collected, thereby removing the incentive to chase significance. Others require authors to share their data and code, so that critics can retrace each step. Large collaborative projects, in which dozens of laboratories run the same protocol, have begun to supply the kind of cumulative evidence that no individual study can provide. Early indications are encouraging, although it would be premature to conclude that the underlying problem has been solved.

Not everyone accepts the pessimistic reading, however. Some scholars contend that a failed replication does not automatically refute the original finding: subtle differences in participants, setting or even the era in which a study is conducted may legitimately alter the outcome. On this view, the low replication rate reflects the complexity of human behaviour rather than any flaw in the method. Critics of this position respond that if an effect is so fragile that it vanishes when the conditions shift slightly, its practical significance must be negligible, and the original claims were framed far too broadly.

There is, moreover, a cultural dimension that technical fixes alone cannot address. Researchers who share their raw data, publish null results or openly correct their own errors currently take a professional risk, because the prevailing system rewards novelty and confidence rather than caution. Until funding bodies, hiring committees and journals treat careful, unglamorous work as a mark of distinction, the incentives that produced the problem will continue to operate, and well-designed procedures will merely be circumvented by those who feel the pressure most acutely.

What, then, should the general reader make of a headline announcing that a new study 'proves' some surprising link between diet and mood? Perhaps the most sensible response is a measured scepticism. A single study, however carefully conducted, is better understood as a contribution to an ongoing conversation than as a verdict. Findings gain credibility as they are corroborated by independent teams, using different methods and different populations, and the more counter-intuitive the claim, the stronger the evidence ought to be. Science, in this respect, is not a collection of facts but a process of progressively eliminating error, and its authority derives from its willingness to expose its own weaknesses.

listening.title: Feedback on two drafts
listening.intro: Listen to the tutorial session. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Right, I've read both of your drafts, and I'd like to start with the introduction, Mei.
Of course. I was worried it was a bit too bold. I wrote that social media causes teenage anxiety.
Well, that's precisely the issue. The evidence doesn't really support such a categorical claim. I'd say it may contribute to anxiety in some adolescents, but causation is another matter.
So you'd recommend something like 'the findings suggest an association'?
Exactly. And I'd add 'to some extent', because the effect sizes are modest.
Fair enough. What about Tomás's section? I thought it read very smoothly.
It does flow, but you rely on 'this' far too often. In the third paragraph, 'this' refers to three different things. Name the noun: 'this trend', 'this discrepancy'.
I see. I'd been trying to avoid repeating myself.
Understandable, but clarity outweighs elegance here. Also, the sentence beginning 'due to the fact the sample was small' is missing a 'that'. Better still, just say 'because'.
Noted. Should I also cut the long list of nominalizations? A friend says my style is a little heavy.

Some of it is perfectly acceptable. 'The expansion of the network' is fine. But 'the carrying out of the implementation of the evaluation' is not. Keep the people in the sentence when it matters who did what.
And the deadline? Is it still Friday?
I'm afraid it has been brought forward to Thursday noon. Send me the revised drafts by then, and we'll go through the conclusions together.
